slide.title: AI Plans, You Decide
slide.body: Monday-to-Friday planner grid with task cards; a hand moves one card to Monday (teal highlight). Small tag: AI for Everyday Work · Lesson 9.

scenes.voiceover: It is Monday morning. You have fifteen things to do, some urgent, some large, and some you have avoided for weeks. An AI assistant can turn that list into a neat plan in seconds. But only you know which task really cannot be late.

slide.title: Way 1: From messy list to plan
slide.body: Jumbled sticky notes on the left → arrow → neat Monday-to-Friday plan on the right, with similar tasks grouped by colour.

scenes.voiceover: This is week three, where we redesign your work week. In this lesson, AI helps you organise your work in three ways. First, it can turn a messy list into a plan. It can group similar tasks, suggest an order, and spread the work across the days.

slide.title: Way 2: Checklists
slide.body: AI suggests the steps · You add what is missing · You remove what does not apply. Example: preparing a meeting.

scenes.voiceover: Second, it can suggest checklists for tasks with many small steps, such as preparing a meeting or welcoming a new team member. You add the steps it missed and remove the ones that do not apply.

slide.title: Way 3: Reusable templates
slide.body: A template page with headings (Updates · Decisions · Actions) and empty spaces to fill in, with a circular arrow labelled 'every week'.

scenes.voiceover: Third, it can build reusable templates for tasks you repeat, such as a weekly status update or a meeting agenda. The template has headings and spaces to fill in, so you do not start from a blank page each week.

slide.title: A planning prompt
slide.body: Here is my task list for next week. Group similar tasks, suggest a priority order and spread them across Monday to Friday. I have about 5 hours per day for this work. Show it as a table with Day, Task and Why this order.

scenes.voiceover: Here is a useful planning prompt. It asks the assistant to group the tasks, suggest a priority order, and spread them across the week, with your available hours per day. It also asks for a table with a column called why this order.

slide.title: What the AI cannot see
slide.body: Your deadlines · Your manager's priorities · Who is waiting for you · Tasks that depend on other teams · Days you are on leave

scenes.voiceover: That why column matters. It shows the assistant's reasoning, so you can see where it guessed. Remember, it does not know your deadlines, your manager's priorities, or which task depends on another team. It may put an easy task first because it looks quick.
So here is the rule for this lesson. AI can suggest an order, but you decide the priorities.

scenes.stock_query: two people arranging sticky notes planning board
scenes.voiceover: Think of a planning partner who arranges the pieces on the table. They put the pieces in a neat order quickly. But you know which pieces matter most, because you know the deadlines and the people.

slide.title: Remove names first
slide.body: Before: real client, colleague and project names (red). After: 'Client A report' · 'Project X' · 'Colleague B' (green).

scenes.voiceover: And before you paste any task list, replace the names of clients, colleagues and projects with general labels, such as client A report or project X. As always, follow your employer's AI policy.

scenes.stock_query: non-profit office worker planning week laptop
scenes.voiceover: Let's see an example. Oksana is a programme assistant at a non-profit organisation in Lviv, in Ukraine. Her list for next week has twelve tasks, including a report for a donor, booking a venue for volunteer training, and the Friday team meeting agenda.

slide.title: The AI's plan
slide.body: Weekly grid: Monday 'Update contact list (quick and easy)' · Thursday 'Donor report (Donor A)'. Other tasks spread across the week.

scenes.voiceover: She replaces the donor's real name with donor A, and pastes the list with the planning prompt. The AI puts update contact list on Monday morning, because it is quick and easy. It puts the donor report on Thursday.

slide.title: Change 1: The donor report
slide.body: AI: Thursday → Oksana: Monday and Tuesday. Why: manager reviews on Wednesday; donor receives it on Thursday.

scenes.voiceover: Oksana changes two things and writes down why. First, she moves the donor report to Monday and Tuesday. The AI did not know that her manager must review it on Wednesday, before it goes to the donor on Thursday.

slide.title: Change 2: The venue booking
slide.body: AI: later in the week → Oksana: Monday. Why: venues book up quickly; the training date cannot change.

scenes.voiceover: Second, she moves the venue booking to Monday. Venues in her city book up quickly at this time of year, and she knows the training date cannot change.

slide.title: A template for every Friday
slide.body: Team meeting agenda: Updates · Decisions · Actions. Edited once, saved, reused weekly.

scenes.voiceover: Then she asks for a reusable agenda template for the Friday team meeting, with headings for updates, decisions and actions. She edits it once and saves it to use every week.

scenes.on_screen_text: Neat is not the same as correct
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to accept the AI's plan because it looks organised. But a neat plan is not the same as a correct plan. Read the why behind each choice, change what conflicts with what you know, and write down your reason.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Plans · checklists · templates. 2. You decide the priorities. 3. Remove names; ask 'why this order'.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, AI can turn a messy list into a weekly plan, suggest checklists and draft reusable templates. Second, the assistant does not know your deadlines, dependencies or people, so you decide the final priorities. Third, remove client, colleague and project names before pasting a task list, and ask the AI to explain its order so you can see where it guessed.

Your turn. In the exercise below this video, paste your real task list for next week, with sensitive details removed, and ask for a prioritised plan. Change at least two of its choices and write down why. Your capstone starts in the next lesson, Map Your Tasks: Where AI Helps and Where It Does Not. See you there.
